name: MacDonald of Kingsburgh
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: DW Stewart recorded this pattern in his 'Old and Rare Scottish Tartans' based on a fragment of a waistcoat given to Prince Charles Edward Stuart (PCE) by MacDonald of Kingsburgh during his wanderings after Culloden. Considered too bright for his use PCE exchanged it with one Malcolm Macleod of Macleod who, before his capture by Government forces, hid it in a rock cleft. After his release a year later he retrieved it but only a small scrap had survived undamaged. Stewart’s reconstruction was woefully inaccurate.

Peter MacDonald adds in July 2004 'The sample is from the Coulson Bonnar collection where it is named MacDonald of Loch Mhaddy' Lochmaddy is a sea loch and settlement in the north east corner of North Uist in the Outer Hebrides.

name: MacDonald of Sleat
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Scottish Tartan Society notes: The MacDonald of Sleat tartan was manufactured in the 18th century and called MacDonald of Sleat, Lord of the Isles. The pattern was devised from an old MacDonald tartan that is shown in a painting at Armadale Castle, but it appears that the reconstruction differs somewhat from the original. Whether this was intended or simply a mistake is entirely open to conjecture but it would not be the first new design to have arisen from an error in the threadcount. Sample in Scottish Tartans Authority Dalgety Collection. This is the same as Middleton - see #903 (original Scottish Tartans Authority reference).

name: MacDonald of The Isles
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Green lightened to show sett. Scottish Tartans Society notes: The design first appeared in the Vestiarium Scoticum and is different from earlier setts attributed to the Lord of the Isles or to any of the Clan Donald branches. It is not generally regarded as a clan tartan. The Sobieski Stuart brothers who published the Vestiarium claimed to be the heirs to a manuscript once in the hands of Prince Charles Edward Stuart himself but the original was never produced for public examination. The book appears to be a curious mixture of fact and fiction in keeping with the romantic ideology of the time. Lochcarron swatch.

registrationNotes: The pattern books of the old firm of weavers, Wilson's of Bannockburn provide a reliable early source for this tartan. Wilson's were in business with a monopoly to supply tartan to the regiments in the second half of the 18th century before this pattern was recorded. Wilsons of Bannockburn a weaving firm founded c1770 near Stirling. The Pattern books are in the National Museum of Antiquities, Edinburgh. Copys of the Pattern books and letters in the Scottish Tartans Society archive.

registrationNotes: According to D.C. Stewart, "It will be observed that the MacDuff tartan is substantially the Royal Stuart with the white and yellow lines removed. Whether this indicates it as a source of the Stuart, or the association of the Earls of Fife with the Crown, remains to be determined." James Logan published this sett in his book, 'The Scottish Gael' in 1831.

name: MacDuff #6
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Scottish Tartans Society notes: In early sources there are many small variations of this design, particularly in the shades and width of the red and blue bands. W and A Smith in their 1850 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland' give this sett and say 'Our authority for this Tartan is 'use and wont'. It is universally worn in the North as MacDuff, it has always been known by the 'Trade' as such; and upon a late occasion, when, in honour of Her Majesty, there was one of those grand fetes given at Braemar, called a 'Gathering,' the numerous retainers of General Duff and many others were attired in this Tartan.'

name: MacGregor of Glenstrae
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This sett appears in the text of the Vestiarium Scoticum, 1829-1890 but is not illustrated. Glen Straye (Glenstrae) lies in the heart of Campbell country and was the scene of a notable period in the history of Clan Gregor which led to the proscription of the name.

name: MacGregor of Glengyle
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Woven on Deeside c.1750. A sample is in the McGregor Hastie Collection which can be found in the Scottish Tartans Society Museum artefact reference B18/6. Notes (May 2006) from Sir Malcom MacGregor of MacGregor, Chief of Clan MacGregor explains that the MacGregor of Deeside and the MacGregor of Glengyle are really one and the same. He has a specimen of this tartan (BLACK and red) which his grandfather obtained from Skeoch Cumming in 1922, who got it from an old woman in Nairn who said it was the tartan of the MacGregors of Glengyle whence her people came. The Chief said 'My father believed this to be correct, bearing in mind the history of the MacGregors of Deeside. The MacGregors transported to Aberdeenshire by the Earl of Moray who came from his estates in Menteith to fight the Mackintoshes in about 1624, were almost certainly MacGregors of Glengyle and would have worn that tartan. Another specimen of this sett is in the possession of Andersons of Edinburgh, believed to date from 1750. It is in red and blue colours as opposed to red and black. Red and black would be a logical extension of the Red and Black discussed above (#1504, original Scottish Tartans Authority reference) so why there is blue instead of black is a mystery.'

registrationNotes: A tartan for the members of the MacHatters of the Old Pueblo, an official chapter of the Red Hat Society which encourages all the ladies in its chapter to wear purple with a red hat. The tartan is designed to showcase those colours. The name is a pun on Mad Hatters (from Alice in Wonderland) and there appear to be such Mad Hatter clubs throughout the US. Old Pueblo is in Tuscon, Arizona.

name: MacIngust

name: MacInnes
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Threadcount recorded by William McInnes in the Public Register of all Arms and Bearings in Scotland, 44/73, 15 November 1960. The Scottish Tartans Society notes for this tartan attribute the design to the 'Onich Grocer' with no further explanation. Further research by Alasdair 'MacInnes' Campbell of Fort William has identified John MacInnes of Onich, who was born around 1851 and was Registrar for Ballachulish and Corran of Ardgour 1874-1920. John MacInnes was also a tailor and weaver and ran a general merchant store from the same premises as his Registry Office. It is said that when King Edward VII was the Prince of Wales he called at John's 'Nether Lochaber Stores' to have an outfit made. It is said that the royal patronage went to John's head - to the disdain of his neighbours.

Wilsons of Bannockburn was a weaving firm founded c1770 near Stirling. The Pattern books are in the National Museum of Antiquities, Edinburgh. Copies of the Pattern books and letters are in the Scottish Tartans Society archive.

registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Threadcount recorded by Kenneth F Mackenzie in the Public Register of all Arms and Bearings in Scotland, 37/127, 27 December 1949. The Mackenzie is the regimental tartan of the Seaforth Highlanders, who were raised by MacKenzie, Earl of Seaforth, in 1778. The clan held lands in Ross-shire and around Muir of Ord, but in the 12th century, they were removed to Wester Ross, (Kintail). The chiefly line of Kintail died out (as prophesised by the Brahan Seer) and the MacKenzies of Cromarty were recognised as Chiefs of the Clan. Wilson's 1819 pattern book records various widths and weights of cloth suitable for the different ranks in the regiment. In 'The Clan and Family Tartans of Scotland' (1850), W and A Smith of Mauchline wrote: 'Both the 71st and 78th Regiments now wear the Tartan common to the MacLeods and the MacKenzies.' This sett is also recorded in Clans Originaux (1880).

This tartan is based on the Mackenzie with the red lines representing 'our shared Scottish blood yet divided by the white and blue of the oceans.' Woven by Marjorie Warren.

registrationNotes: The McKerrell of Hillhouse family tartan incorporates the colours of the family coat of Arms - gold, blue, red and silver (white). The McKerrell of Hillhouse and the Dress version can be worn by all those with the name McKerrell and its spelling variations, with the permission of McKerrell of Hillhouse. The earliest illustration of the tartan is in a portrait by de Sange of Robert McKerrell of Hillhouse, 1804-1875. The tartan was recorded in the Lyon Court Books (LCB) 42 on the 25th June 1982. The tartan has been woven in a smaller sett for use in trews.

name: MacKessog
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The MacKessog tartan was designed in 2006 to commemorate the saint who came to Loch Lomondside in 510 AD to bring Christianity to the people of Argyll. Saint Kessog founded a monastery on the island of Inch Tavannach and a church in Luss nearly 1,500 years ago. In his memory Redshanke of Inverary has designed this tartan which has been woven on the Isle of Islay. The tartan is exclusive to the Church and Pilgrimage Centre of Luss. The tartan is based on the Bruce sett due to the veneration of Kessog by King Robert the Bruce, who led his soldiers into the battle of Bannockburn in the name of the blessed Kessog and established Luss as a major pilgrimage site during the Middle Ages. The colours are : two shades of green for the hills, blue for the loch, a white stripe to create the Scottish saltire, a purple stripe for the heather and for Kessog's ecclesiastical significance, and a red stripe for his martyrdom. The saint was murdered in 520 AD at Bandry, a small village just south of Luss. All pilgrims visiting Luss and those who choose to be married here are entitled to wear the MacKessog tartan as their own. A woven sample is preserved by the Scottish Tartans Authority.

registrationNotes: The MacKinlay tartan could be described in tartan parlance as Black Watch with red. It is similar to the early military setts produced by Wilson's of Bannockburn for the MacKenzies, the MacLeods and the Gordons, but there is no mention in Wilson's comprehensive pattern books of a MacKinlay tartan. There are, however, grounds for comparison with the Farquharson, as MacKinlays are named in that clan. To further confuse the issue the sett is identical to Logan's 'Murray of Athol'. W & A.K.Johnston, The Tartans of the Clans and Septs of Scotland, 1906.

name: MacKintosh (Chief)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Scarlett count used (261). Logan wrote 'The Chief also wears a particular taran of a very showy pattern' and the Smiths of Mauchline illustrated it in their 1850 book 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans & Families of Scotland' commenting 'We have every reason to believe that this Tartan is the genuine set which has been worn by the Chiefs of this distinguished Clan, for many generations. Our reason for giving it, as well as some others which have similar claims to a place in our work, is that the Chief did, in some instances, wear a Tartan different from his Clan - which sets were also considered hereditary.' If the 'many generations' claim is correct and we assume three generations then that would place this tartan in the mid 1700s. Also known as Clan Chattan and with a white line on the red ground, as Clan Chattan Chief. Very close indeed to MacPherson tartan at #682 (original Scottish Tartans Authority reference). Sample in Scottish Tartans Authority's Dalgety Collection.

registrationNotes: Scottish Tartans Society notes: This sett appears in D C Stewarts book, The Setts of the Scottish Tartans, with slightly different proportions. The Lyon Court Book No. 1 records the sett in relation to the narrowest stripe. ie Y 1, Vt (Vert meaning green) 10 1/2, Bu 5, etc. The rendering illustrated here multiplies the Lyon count by two. Commercially manufactured cloth may vary from these proportions. D C Stewart calls the sett 'a modern arrangement'.

name: MacKirdy
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This sample comes from the MacGregor-Hastie collection which forms the basis of the cloth archive of the Scottish Tartans Society. MacGregor-Hastie noted, 'A pattern seen at Andersons, Edinburgh, was labelled 'MacKirdy'. It is a simple green tartan. The family are usually given as a sept of the Stuarts of Bute. The tartan is modern. One can assume that the sample dates between 1930 and 1950. At a very early period the larger part of the Island of Bute belonged to the Mackuerdys, which was leased to them by King James 1V of Scotland.

name: Mackison
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed in January 2007 by Steven Mackison who is hoping to 'get the Mackisons recognised as a clan' by Lord Lyon. The Tartan is a modification of the Menteith district Tartan. The Mackisons trace their name to St. Mackessog (Mackessan) the original patron Saint of Scotland, an Irish Missionary Bishop who settled in and around Luss and other areas of Lomondside. The Mackisons begin as residents of Menteith district and latterly were popoulous in Perthshire, particularly in the parish of Kilmadock. The thread-counts from the Menteith tartan have been reversed with green becoming dark blue and blue becoming green. The white in the Menteith has been with a purple, indicative of St. Mackessan's status as a Bishop.

registrationNotes: A colour variation of Black Watch tartan that was first recorded in James Logan’s The Scottish Gael, 1831 but likely to have been a Wilsons of Bannockburn design. In their 1850 book 'The Clan and Family Tartans of Scotland' W and A Smith of Mauchline wrote: 'There are several Fancy MacLachlan Tartans in the market, but we have no hesitation in giving this as the genuine Tartan. A lady of very high rank obtained the cloth for us from a member of the family - besides which, it has been confirmed by all the authorities we have consulted.' Of the three distinct versions of MacLachlan tartan, this is the one most often woven today.

name: MacLaren
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Wilsons of Bannockburn were producing this tartan before 1820 under the name of 'Pattern No.232 or Regent' but with purple in place of blue. The Regency ended when George IV succeeded to the throne in that year and the pattern was adopted by the MacLarens at the time of the visit of the King to Edinburgh in 1822. Wilsons replaced their purple with blue by 1830 and were selling it as MacLaren. The tartan has been adopted by the Small Arms School Corps with permission of the Clan Chief.

It was included in their 1819 Key Pattern Book under the name ‘Pattern No.232 or Regent’ in recognition of the Prince Regent. When the Prince became King George IV in 1820 the name became redundant. It was adopted by the MacLarens c.1822 and the purple replaced by blue, the version worn today by the clan.

registrationNotes: Threadcount estimated from a portrait at Dunvegan Castle, Isle of Skye, of the 24th chief, John Norman, painted posthumously in 1835. John Norman is shown in the costume worn for the visit of George IV to Edinburgh in 1822. The portrait includes a snuff-box on the table painted in this tartan.

name: MacLeod/MacNicol
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This is the MacNicol tartan which, for some reason, was recorded as MacLeod/MacNicol in two private collections of tartans compiled in the 1950s.

name: McDougall, Miss Anne (Personal)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes.
registrationNotes: Designed by Jamie Scarlett MBE and woven by DC Dalgleish for Miss Anne McDougall on the occasion of her marriage to Ruari Halford-MacLeod, 28 July 1978.

name: MacLeod - 1906 (Black & Red)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: W & A K Johnston, The Tartans of the Clans and Septs of Scotland, 1906.

name: MacLeod – 1906 (Black & White)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Published in W & A.K. Johnston's 1906 2 Vol work and detailed in Ruairidh MacLeod's 'The Tartans of Clan MacLeod'. Called MacLeod Black & White or Mourning. There are observers who state that attaching the label 'Mourning' to sombre tartans was a Victorian affectation.

name: MacLeod of Argentina
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed in 1978 by Murdo MacLeod of Murdo MacLeod's Fabrics Ltd in Stornoway to celebrate Scotland's football team playing in the World Cup. Named after the team manager Ally MacLeod. Ian Zaczek in his World Tartans book (2001) makes no mention of these facts and states that it is the tartan of the Argentinian branch of the MacLeod Clan Society. Perhaps it has been subsequently adopted by that society but there is no evidence of that and the pipe band still wears the Royal Stewart.

name: MacLeod of Assynt
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: From W & A K Johnston 1906 book. This is essentially the same as MacLeod of Harris but omits the black guards to the yellow stripe.

name: MacLeod of California
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed by Frank B Cannonito from Calfornia and DC Dalgliesh Ltd as a dress tartan. Based on the hunting MacLeod and Baillie Fencible tartans. Approved by the Clan Chief.

name: MacLeod of Gesto #2
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: A sample in the Provost MacBean collection, now in the Scottish Tartans Authority archive.

name: MacLeod of Gesto #1
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Details from a hard tartan sample in The Scottish Tartan Authority's collection with an undated old and indistinct label saying "McLeod of Gesto. Produced by Ian Hilleary, Tayinloan Lodge, Bernisdale Lodge, Isle of Skye."

name: MacLeod of Lewis
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Published in the Vestiarium Scoticum (1842) where it is named simply ‘MacLeod’. Also known as MacLeod Dress and sometimes jokingly referred to as 'Loud MacLeod'.

name: MacLeod of Raasay
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Details from a sample in the collection of the Highland Society of London collated (1906-30).

name: MacLeod of Skye
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Documented in the W & A K Johnston 1906 book where it is given this name. It is essentially the same as MacLeod of Gesto (#280) but the black guards have moved from the red to the yellow stripe.

name: MacLeod Red
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed after the tartan worn by Norman MacLeod, 22nd Chief of the clan, painted by Allan Ramsay in 1747, with the costume painted by Van Haecken (see details in entry for MacLeod 'Portrait'). A yellow stripe was added by Ruairidh MacLeod to enhance the family resemblance to other MacLeod tartans, and to differentiate this from Murray of Tullibardine, the name now attached to the sett in the portrait. It was agreed at a clan Parliament in 1982 chaired by clan chief John MacLeod of MacLeod that this tartan be adopted as an official red MacLeod.

name: MacLeod Society of Scotland
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The MacLeod Society of Scotland tartan was designed in 1991 by Trudi Mann of Wick for the Clan MacLeod Centenary and was accepted by the Chief as the Society sett.

name: MacLeod Special Dress (Dance)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes. Prepared for weaving by D C Dalgliesh Ltd.
registrationNotes: There is no known official MacLeod dress. This is a Dance tartan from D C Dalgliesh of Selkirk.

name: Macleod, Winnifred Mary, Dress
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes.
registrationNotes: Presented to a descendent of Winnifred Mary MacLeod to commerate Winnifred's life. Designed by Jessica Maclead-Dent and MacIsaac Kiltmakers. It can be used by Highland dancers with permission - Family Restricted.

name: MacLeod's Highlanders
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Threadcount taken from a Wilsons of Bannockburn pattern book. William Wilsons was a weaving firm founded c1770 at Bannockburn near Stirling. The pattern books are held by National Museums Scotland, Edinburgh. Copies of the pattern books and correspondence are in the Scottish Tartans Society archive. See also 42nd Regt - Drummers' Plaid at SRT #283.

name: MacLintock - 1880
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Details from a specimen in Clans Originaux , 1880. The MacLintocks are claimed by Clan MacDougall as well as Clan Colquhoun as a dependent family name.

name: MacLoughlin of Ardmarnoch (Personal)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Dr Paul MacLoughlin described his reason for wanting a tartan of his own as, 'daughters with eccentric tastes'. This sett which is based on the Black Watch, has the red stripe from the MacLachlan. This is a private family tartan.

name: MacLulich
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This threadcount was taken by the Scottish Tartans Society from a McGregor Hastie sample. It is exactly the same threadcount and colours as STR #3944 (original Scottish Tartans Authority reference) Stewart, Blue. The same sett with changed colours is also recorded as Macbeth.

name: MacManus (Estimated threadcount)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: One of a series of Irish name tartans designed by Scotch Corner of Gateshead, England.

name: MacMaster (USA) #2
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Proposed by 'MacMaster Associates' Utica, New York, USA, for use by all with the name.

name: MacMedic
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Worn at the First Aid Post at the Stone Mountain Games. Georgia, USA 1997.

name: MacMichael
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed by Philip D. Smith, 1991. Not known if Personal or Clan/Family.

name: MacMillan Anc (Clans Originaux)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Asymmetric woven sample in 1880 Clans Originaux. Count estimated (Scottish Tartans Authority June 2004) from colour photo so not very accurate. Different warp and weft - green blocks are rectangles instead of squares. See also #2025 (original Scottish Tartans Authority reference).

name: MacMillan Ancient
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The term 'ancient' normally describes a change in colour that can be applied to any tartan. In the case of MacMillan the 'ancient' form involves a more radical change, justifying the traditional use of the adjective in the name of the tartan. James Logan, co-author of 'The Clans of the Scottish Highlands' (1847), states that this version is identical with Buchanan. The thread count was deduced by J. Cant from the illustration by R.R. MacIan in the same work.

name: MacMillan Dress
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: From a comment made by D C Stewart in 'Setts of the Scottish Tartans' (1950) it was assumed that the source of this tartan was the Vestiarium Scoticum - 'All three first appear in the Vestiarium Scoticum' - but in the 2nd edition he corrected the error and it read all two which excluded the MacMillan. In Clans Originaux the woven sample shows the red as being maroon and it is called simply 'MacMillan'.

name: MacMillan Hunting
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The modern Hunting MacMillan incorporates red and yellow stripes from the ancient design with the greens and blues of the Vestiarium version. Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacMillan Hunting #2
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: W & A K Johnstons' 1906 book explains that this tartan was designed and manufactured in 1890 by Baillie Donald Macmillan, J.P. of Partick, a representataive of the Loch Arkaig branch of the clan, and Chieftain of the Clan Macmillan Society. Patented and registered as Breacanseilgmhicgillemhaoil 'it has already attained great popularity, almost completely supplanting the old clan tartan.' Apparently the former President of the Clan MacMillan Society, Major Cameron Macmillan, always referred to this as Baillie Macmillan's tartan. Cameron was a boy in the 1890s when this tartan was a new product issuing from the Baillie's highland outfitting establishment in Partick. It's said that it did not really catch on until the late Chief, General Sir Gordon MacMillan, decided to dress all his family in it to make them easily identifiable from the rest of the clan who wore the Ancient. An idea which rather collapsed by Sir Gordon's move popularising the Hunting sett. A slightly different story is told in the 1906 Johnstons book.

name: MacMillan Society of Glasgow
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Reputed to have been specially designed and woven for the MacMillan Clan Society of Glasgow. Threadcount taken from sample in the MacGregor-Hastie collection in the Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacMillan - 2002 (Black - Unofficial)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This unauthorised and symmetrical version of the traditional asymmetrical MacMillan clan tartan is produced by Marton Mills of Yorkshire. Although not recognised as a MacMillan tartan by the Chief (Jan. 2008), it seems to have gained some popularity in the USA.Originally brought to light by a Graeme Ross of Aberdeen, there may be a sample in the Scottish Tartans Society archives.

name: MacMugen (Personal)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes.
registrationNotes: Created by Bernard MacMugen in 1999. The light colour is un-dyed natural fibre and the dark is natural fibre dyed dark blue with natural indigo. Can be worn by anyone of the name. Original weavers were Geoffrey Tailor of Edinburgh. Woven sample.

name: MacNab (No 199)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: From Wilsons' 1819 Key Pattern Book where it is named No 199 or MacNab.

name: MacNab (VS)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This is the version given by the Sobieski Stuarts in their Vestiarium Scoticum 1842. Like the majority of their designs, there is no other authority for this pattern and unlike some, this tartan was never widely taken up.

name: MacNab (Clan)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This is the usual clan tartan. A specimen is included in the Highland Society of London Collection1815-22 . The structure of the MacNab is identical with that of the Black Watch; but, by a translation of colours, the most subdued of tartans becomes one of the most striking. James Logan recorded this pattern in his book, 'The Scottish Gael' in 1831, despite receiving a different sett from the largest weaving company of the time, William Wilson and Son of Bannockburn – see MacNab #2.

name: MacNab (1950 Trade Version)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: A Trade variation, whether by design or error is unknown, on the basic clan tartan. It was first recorded in a collection compiled in the 1950s and has continued in production from time to time since.

name: MacNab (Old)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This tartan appears in the portrait of Francis MacNab of MacNab by Raeburn c1810. A specimen was included in the Highland Society of London’s collection 1815-22 where it is labelled ‘Old MacNab’. The entry in W and A Smith's 1850 publication 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans & Families of Scotland' reads: 'We received our specimen of the Tartan from the Manufacturer who made it for the old Chief of the Clan.' As a result, this is sometimes (incorrectly) referred to as the ‘Chief’s sett’. The manufacturer would have been Wilsons of Bannockburn who were probably responsible for the design c1800. They regarded this as the genuine MacNab tartan.

name: MacNab, Ancient
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Woven by D.C. Dalgliesh and callled Ancient MacNab. Should be treated as as a fashion tartan according to the wishes of the 23rd Chief. MacNab of MacNab.

name: MacNamara
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Possibly one of the Scotch Corner (Gateshead) series of Irish surname tartans.

name: MacNaughton
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The sett in this form is sometimes used by the Grahams as a dress sett, due to an entry in Wilson's 1847 pattern book designating it as such. It is the opinion of the Society that the single azure stripe is in error. Wilsons of Bannockburn a weaving firm founded c1770 near Stirling. The Pattern books are in the National Museum of Antiquities, Edinburgh. Copies of the Pattern books and letters are in the Scottish Tartans Society archive

name: MacNaughton - 1831
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: James Logan collected information for his book The Scottish Gael between 1826 and 1831. The MacNaughton tartan is also recorded by W and A Smith in their Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland (1850). The Tartan Society entry carries on to say 'Other works contain a commonly reproduced error' but doesn't specify what error. The tartan closely resembles the MacDuff, which may bear out the claim that the MacNaughtons were originally a Moray tribe transplanted by Malcolm IV. The MacNaughton tartan is worn by the Vale of Athol pipe band. Sample in Scottish Tartans Authority's Dalgety Collection.

name: MacNaughton Dress
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Designed by Jim Murray of the Macnaughton Group Ltd (House of Edgar). Approved by the Clan Chief.

name: MacNeil of Barra - Chief
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Originally a Wilsons of Bannockburn fashion tartan, it is included amongst specimens in a sample book date 1838 . In 1997 the Chief of Clan MacNeil wrote that Robert Lister Macneil of Barra adopted this tartan for himself and his family in the 1930s. Threadcount recorded by Ian MacNeil of Barra, Chief of the MacNeils, in the Lyon Court Books (writs section), 122, 12 October 2001.

name: MacNeil Dress
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This sett appears in Paton's of Alloa’s collection of woven samples that date to the early 20th century.

name: MacNeil of Barra
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The official threadcount recorded by Ian MacNeil of Barra, Chief of the MacNeils, in the Lyon Court Books (writs section), 122, 12 October 2001. However, this differs from the original Wilsons’ setting in having narrow black guards to the yellow stripe whereas in Wilsons’ setting that were proportionally three time the size of the yellow.

name: MacNeil of Colonsay #1
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: First show in W & AK Johnsons’ The tartans of the clans and septs of Scotland with the arms of the chiefs. Edinburgh 1906. Threadcount recorded by Ian MacNeil of Barra, Chief of the McNeils, in the Lyon Court Books (writs section), 122, 12 October 2001.

name: MacNeil of Colonsay #2
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Registration notes: Details taken from an undated sample in Vo 2 of the Highland Society of London’s collection gathered between 1906-1934. This version is very like the MacDonald tartan and is quite unlike the present day MacNeil of Colonsay.

name: MacNicol/Nicolson (W & A Smith)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This threadcount is taken from the manuscript of W and A Smith 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland'. The Smith's sources included the findings of George Hunter, an Army clothier, who toured the Highlands in search of old tartans prior to 1822.

name: MacNicol/Nicolson (Inverness Tweed Mill Co Ltd)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: From the records of the Inverness Tweed Mill Co Ltd, Telfer St, Inverness and dated 1869. One of the variations deduced from the McIan drawing of 1845-7. In 1980 the Nicolsons and the MacNicols were recognised as separate clans. When Lord Carnock was recognised as chief of the Nicolsons, Lord Lyon accepted the petition of Ian Nicholson of Scorrybreac, to change his name and re-matriculate his arms as Iain Macneacail of Macneacail and Scorrybreac. Thus the Skye MacNicols are now members of the Clan MacNeacail.

name: MacNiven
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes. Prepared for weaving by D C Dalgliesh Ltd.
registrationNotes: Designed by Frank Cannonito and Kenny R Dalgleish. Based in part on the MacNaughton of which the MacNivens are a Sept. The name in Mr Cannonito's family was spelt, MacKniffen. Other members of the family have dropped the 'Mac' since arriving in America in 1650. This clan tartan was accredited by the Scottish Tartans Society in 1988. Frank and/or his wife also designed the California MacLeod.

name: MacOrrell
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Dalgety Archives: 'Margaret MacDougall (Inverness Museum) said that Fraser of Reelig 'told me that Macorrel was a member of the Rifle Association and always wore this tartan, which he said he had designed for himself about 20 years ago.' Meanwhile, from the Scottish Tartans Society notes: The MacOrrell tartan has similarities with the MacDonald, Lord of the Isles sett, which may point a connection with the name MacDonnell or MacDonald. The name Orr was used by a sept of the MacGregors and also of the Campbells of Argyll, suggesting that the root of the name originated in the Lochaber and Argyll districts. There is an undated sample of the tartan in the cloth archive of the Scottish Tartans Society.

name: MacPhail
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Threadcount taken from a c.1930-50 sample in The Scottish Tartans Authority’s collection.

name: MacPhail (Blue Bands)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Both Scottish Tartans Society index and JCT files give black bands on the red rather than the blue shown here and woven by Ingles Buchan. MacPhail means son of Paul.

name: MacPhail Hunting
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Details from a sample in Clan Originaux (1880) where it is labelled simply 'MacPhail'.

name: MacPhee (Black and White)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: In 1992, Sandy MacPhie, the Commander of the MacPhees wrote from his home in Queensland Australia, inquiring about this tartan. The existence of a black and white pattern was known to him but the precise detail was obscure. The Society had two reported examples of a black and white MacPhee which met the description. One from the researches of a Canadian member, A.C. Lumsden, and the other from a Mr D. Brown in Leeds. It was on the register as a simple 'Noting' and had been for some time. It is now upgraded to 'Registered'.

name: MacPhee MacFee or MacIver
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Sample from D Brown of Leeds March 1969, a Trade sett. Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacPherson
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Old and Rare Scottish Tartans' (1893), contains a selection of forty five setts, woven in silk, of special interest or antiquity. Many of the illustrated tartans owe their present day popularity to the publication of this work. The author was D.W. Stewart.

name: MacPherson #10
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Drawn on squared paper. Sketches of the Clans of Scotland, 1884. Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacPherson #2
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This plate is taken from the manuscript of W and A Smith 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland'. The Smith's sources included the findings of George Hunter, an Army clothier, who toured the Highlands in search of old tartans prior to 1822.

name: MacPherson #3
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Very similar to the MacPherson of Crubin but for a single white stripe. Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacPherson #4
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Sett specified by Capt W.Cheyne-MacPherson of Dalchally as being that of the silk scarf given by Simon Lord Lovat to his daughter on her marriage to Ewan MacPherson. Scotish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacPherson #5
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Wilsons No 43. Same as Kidd (STR #1957).

name: MacPherson #6
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: James Grant took all of the seventy two tartans in his book from actual specimens in use at the time (The Tartans and the Clan of Scotland, 1886). Many are identical to those found in the earlier work of the Smith brothers in 1850. Grant's version shows a slight reduction in the red ground showing the Victorian trend towards more compact setts.

name: MacPherson #7
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This sett is taken from the records of Messrs Bolingbroke and Jones of Norwich, who were weavers around 1870. Some of the tartans have been adopted or modified in recent times as the copyright of the designs is now in the public domain. This Collection is found in the Scottish Tartans Society archive.

name: MacPherson #8
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: This sample comes from the MacGregor-Hastie collection which forms the basis of the cloth archive of the Scottish Tartans Society. Some of the samples, including this one, were unmarked. One can assume that the sample dates between 1930 and 1950.

name: MacPherson (Crubin Plaid)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Examined by D C Stewart in 1947. It is suspected that this is Wilson's Macintosh Old or New from the 1819 pattern book. Thread count halved to show whole sett.

name: MacPherson Dress
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
restrictions: Yes.
registrationNotes: There are a great number of variations of the Dress MacPherson, many of them modern trade designs which are popular with country dancers. Hugh Macpherson of Edinburgh, kiltmaker and tartan designer some decades ago, supplied samples of these to the Scottish Tartan Society around 1980.

name: MacPherson Dress (1842)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: The Sobieskis are said ('Old Cluny' 1962) to have added the yellow line to this sett which was said to have existed 'long before they appeared on the scene' when it was also known as Breacan Glas. It was at one time sold as 'Maggie Lauder' and the suggestion was that it was named after Sir Dick Lauder's daughter - he being a great supporter of the two Sobieski brothers. This version was recorded in the Scottish Tartans Society Sindex without the suffix 'Dress' and with red in place of purple. Manufacturers have consistantly produced a MacPherson Dress with double purple stripes.

name: MacPherson Dress (1951)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: See also STR #2713. This is the sett featured in W and A Smith's 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland' (1850). It is also the sett woven by Lochcarron of Scotland.

registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: D. C. Dalgliesh collection, a weaving firm in Selkirk.

name: MacPherson Dress Red (Dance)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: There are a great number of variations of the Dress MacPherson, many of them modern trade designs which are popular with country dancers. Hugh Macpherson of Edinburgh, kiltmaker and tartan designer, supplied samples of these to the Scottish Tartans Society in around 1980. Hugh departed from his normal practice here and introduced an additional colour with purple tramlines instead of red on the white band.

name: MacPherson Hunting
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: D W Stewart said (in 1893) 'it was the earliest known to have been worn by the clan, and is reputed to have been worn in two forms; as a clan tartan with a white ground and as a hunting tartan with a grey ground. It first appeared in the Smiths' 1850 'Authenticated Tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland' who said of it: 'This pattern, which, upon the Chief's authority, we give as the Hunting MacPherson was made. For the grandmother of the present representative of the family, from an old shawl or plaid, which had been preserved in Cluny Castle for some generations.'

name: MacPherson of Cluny
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Count halved to show sett. Peter MacDonald suggests that Wilson may have named the pattern after Cluny MacPherson of '45 fame as a romantic Highland hero. He also said that in 1817, the chief, Duncan MacPherson, authenticated the Caledonia/Kidd tartan as the correct Clan MacPherson tartan, apparently unaware of this sett, although this was perhaps for his own use.

name: MacPherson of Cluny (Black and White)
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: Said to be the threadcount registered with the Lord Lyon but this does not appear in the Lord Lyon's books. This is the same as ITI #1872 but with the yellow line between the two whites, replaced with white. Cluny MacPherson had this to say about it to the Smith brothers in 1850: 'The light one enclosed by you was known as Breacan Glas (the Pied Wagtail) long before John Stuart (one of the Sobieski brothers) was heard of in this country, although I rather think the addition of the yellow stripe was introduced by him, or rather taken from his MS; but at all events the Tartan is an old MacPherson.'

name: MacPhie/Macfie
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: First seen in the 1880 Clans Originaux (as McPhee) and then in the W & A.K. Johnston book of 1906. As officially approved by Commander A C 'Sandy' McPhie, and as recorded by Court of Lord Lyon LCB 79 dated 29th August 1991. Lyon count: W/Y2 R24 G4 R2 G32 MacPhies, MacFie, or MacDuffie held lands on the Isle of Colonsay until the mid seventeenth century but were later scattered by the clearances. They were the hereditary Keeper of the Records to the Lords of the Isles. The present Commander, Sandy MacPhie, lives in Queensland, Australia. The resemblance of this tartan to that of the Camerons may denote the MacFies' allegiance to that clan on the mainland after they were dispersed from Colonsay.

It is this tartan that is recorded in the Lyon Court books. A darker coloured version of MacThomas tartan was produced by David Thomas, one time director of the Strathmore Woollen Co, Forfar, in the 1950s and approved by the then MacThomas Chief. Both versions of MacThomas tartan were adopted by the MacThomas Clan Society, when it was founded in 1954. A revised threadcount was recorded by the Clan Chief in Lyon Court Book no.36, 27th June 1979, correcting a minor numerical error in an earlier recording.

name: Maine, Original State of
registrationDate: This tartan was recorded prior to the launch of The Scottish Register of Tartans.
registrationNotes: A confusing situation. The Maine tartan is the oldest of American 'state' tartans. Designed 1964 by Sol Gilis of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia and originally woven by the Maine Spinning Company which has now gone out of business. When the tartan was first introduced it was reported in the Glasgow Herald (30.12.65) that it had been 'duly accredited by the State of Maine'. The State archives, however, are unable to locate the authorization. The tartan dropped out of sight and was then re-discovered in 1987 and then woven in Maine in 1988 by Jane Holmes of Plymouth, ME and items made from the fabric are made and sold by her company, the Maine Tartan and Tweed Co. The Maine State Tartan was copyrighted in 1988 by the MTTCo. Items made out of the Maine Tartan are also available from the Maine State Museum Gift Shop in Augusta, My Maine Bag in Bangor, and Just Me in Portland. Since this #502 is not the official Maine tartan (that is #3068, original Scottish Tartans Authority references), the foregoing information (taken from the Internet in June 2006) is confusing. The later variation of this (Maine Dirigo #3068, original Scottish Tartans Authority reference) has been adopted as the official State of Maine Tartan in January 2001.

registrationNotes: There is an error in D.C. Stewarts, 'The Setts..' (1950 1st Edition) corrected in the 2nd edition (1974). The name Malcolm was established, as distinct from MacCallum, in 1770 when the 9th Chief of Poltalloch changed the family name to Malcolm. This may well be the sett on which the MacCallum was based "from the recollection of old people in Argyllshire" and which D.W. Stewart illustrated in silk in his book, 'Old and Rare..'. Wilson's of Bannockburn produced a symmetrical version of the Malcolm tartan. W.& A.Smith Authenticated tartans of the Clans and Families of Scotland 1850.
